content: 1. Ten high-income countries, five upper middle-income countries, fourteen lower middle-income countries, and eleven low-income countries reported that no blood was collected from donors under the age of 18. Similarly, twenty-nine countries (five high-income, four upper middle-income, nine lower middle-income, and eleven low-income) reported no blood donations from donors aged 65 years and above due to age restrictions outlined in donation criteria. 2. Age-specific population data (16–18 years or 65–70 years) from these countries were excluded from the calculation of the average age group-specific donation rate by World Bank economic group. 3. A total of 110 countries (35 in Europe, 31 in Africa, 18 in the Western Pacific, 11 in the Americas, 10 in the Eastern Mediterranean, and 5 in South-East Asia) provided data on the number of voluntary non-remunerated whole blood donations from first-time and repeat donors. 4. Several European countries have implemented a policy of testing without collecting blood from first-time donors, resulting in 100% of their blood collections being from repeat donors. 5. The proportion of whole blood donations by repeat voluntary non-remunerated donors varies by WHO region. For example, in South-East Asia, the range is 2–100%, while in the Western Pacific, it is 12–85%. 6. The frequency of donations per donor per year serves as a proxy measure for regular blood donation. However, this may underestimate the actual donation frequency, as 48 countries reported identical numbers for active donors and donations, likely due to the absence of a robust donor database capable of uniquely identifying donations from the same donor. 7. In 2013, 64 countries reported a total of 101,994 autologous blood donations. However, many countries could not provide data on autologous donations, as these are often collected in hospitals, and many nations lack systems for data collection or reporting on hospital activities. Consequently, the reported total number of autologous blood donations is likely an underestimation. 8. Blood collected in an anticoagulant can be stored and transfused as whole blood or separated into components (e.g., red cell concentrates, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and platelet concentrates) to meet the needs of multiple patients. Globally, 85% of whole blood donations were processed into components, with significant variation by income level and WHO region. 9. In 2013, 97% of whole blood donations in high-income countries were processed into components, compared to 92% in upper middle-income countries, 59% in lower middle-income countries, and 50% in low-income countries. The lowest percentages were observed in the South-East Asia Region (61%) and the Eastern Mediterranean Region (65%). 10. Across WHO regions, the proportion of whole blood donations processed into components varied widely. For example, in Europe, over 90% of donations were processed into components in nearly all countries, while in Africa, only 36% of countries reported processing less than 25% of donations into components. 11. Laboratory screening policies for blood donations include testing for HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV). Of 180 responding countries, 176 reported policies for screening all blood donations for HIV, HBV, and HCV. However, variations exist in the specific tests used, such as serological testing, nucleic acid amplification testing (NAT), and antigen/antibody testing. 12. For syphilis, 173 countries reported policies for testing all blood donations, while two European countries (Denmark and Iceland) do not routinely test for syphilis. Norway tests all new donors for syphilis. 13. Eighteen countries in Latin America reported policies for testing all blood donations for Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease), while twelve countries conduct selective testing for donors with travel history to at-risk areas or defined risk factors. 14. Thirty-seven countries reported policies for testing blood donations for human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV).
